name: Karl Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a company of about a hundred and twenty people that makes payroll software for small businesses, places like bakeries, garages and building firms. I'm on the payslip team: the part that turns hours and tax rules into the payslip a worker gets. Every spring the tax rates change and we all go a bit grey updating the tables and checking that nobody's pay comes out wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. If our code is wrong, a bricklayer gets short-paid, and I take that seriously. What wears me out is that I'm not quick. My lead, Ines, can read a tax rule and see the problem in a minute, and it takes me an afternoon. I'm on the lower pay band and I've got a couple of weeks of savings, and that's with my girlfriend Paula and me splitting everything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, once I saw others using them safely. Mostly to tidy up the wording of a message or explain an error. I don't let it near tax tables; that's too important. My dad runs a plumbing and heating business with my older brother, and he still does his quotes on paper, so I'm the modern one in the family, which is funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. A lot of people got excited about a shortcut, and it turns out there wasn't one. I'd probably say it to my dad over Sunday lunch, and he'd say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on as I am, which is fine, but I'm not going to get rich at this rate. I'm on low pay, savings of two weeks, and only a handful of software companies within an hour's train. My real worry is whether I'm good enough to get to the next pay band in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder at the tax rules, maybe ask Ines if I can take on the spring update next year as my own project. I'd keep using the AI tool for small stuff only. Paula and I would start putting a little aside each month, maybe sixty, because we want to get engaged and that costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the ordinary kind. I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad and brother are in plumbing. Have you ever thought about joining them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's asked more than once. I always said no, because I wanted to do something different and he wanted that for me too, really. But it's always there in the back of my mind, like a spare tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'standing still' cost you and Paula?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, mainly. Paula's a teaching assistant, so neither of us earns much. If I'm on the same pay in five years, we're renting at forty and that's not the life either of us grew up with.

say: People got excited about a **shortcut**, and there **wasn't one**.
Now we can **get back to work**, and my dad would say he told me so.
think: I'm on **low pay** with two weeks of savings and few nearby software firms.
My real worry is reaching the **next pay band** in two years.
do: Ask Ines to let me own the **spring tax update** next year.
Keep using the AI tool for **small stuff only**.
Save about **sixty a month** with Paula toward getting engaged.
feel: **Ordinary unease**: scared of **standing still**, not of robots.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of robots, I'm scared of standing still.
fieldNote: Karl's family **plumbing firm** sits in his mind like a spare tyre.
His worry is **slow progress** and never owning a house.
He uses AI only once it's **proven** and keeps it away from tax tables.

steps.text: Ask Ines to lead next spring's tax table update
Save sixty a month with Paula toward an engagement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to do what keeps them competitive, that's how it works. But I'd also say they owe it to people to train them, not just let them go. Apprenticeships for grown-ups, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the payslip team gets smaller. Checking tax rules and writing the code to match is exactly what these tools are getting good at. Ines will be fine. The question is whether they need a slow junior next to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I could see the tools were safe on real payroll, I'd learn them properly, probably by copying how Ines uses them. I'd start doing Saturdays with my dad and brother, learning the basics of heating work, so the spare tyre's actually pumped up. And Paula and I would put the engagement off a year and save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing two things at once and not sure which one I'd end up in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad react if you started coming on Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would pretend my Saturdays in the plumbing business were nothing and be quietly delighted. My brother would make fun of me for the first month, then give me all the jobs in lofts. That's how it goes in our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies should train people, not just let them go. Who should pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that save the money, mostly. I don't want the government handing out cheques. But if a firm cuts ten people because a tool does their work, it can pay for a few of them to learn something new.

say: Companies have to stay **competitive**; that's how it works.
They owe staff **training**, like apprenticeships for grown-ups, not just letting them go.
think: The **payslip team** gets smaller, because checking tax rules is what tools do well.
The question is whether they need a **slow junior** beside Ines.
do: Learn the AI tools by **copying Ines** once they're proven safe.

Put the **engagement off** a year and save harder.
feel: **Anxious**, doing two things at once and unsure which one he'll **end up** in.

fieldNote: Karl believes in **markets**, but wants firms that cut jobs to pay for retraining.
He starts turning the family trade into a **real fallback** early.
Putting the **engagement off** shows the money pressure is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and people need to look after their own, families and communities first. I wouldn't be shouting for handouts. I'd be telling young lads to learn a trade, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of software within two years. My whole job is thinking work: tax rules, code, checking. The good thing is I've got a door open, my dad's business, and plumbing is hands-on, so it lasts until robots arrive about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time with my dad within the year, as a trainee, on much less money. I'd start the plumbing qualification at the college straight away. Paula and I would give up the flat and move into my parents' spare room to save rent, and the engagement waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more than scared. I'd have a plan and a family behind me. But I'd lie awake about 2031, when the robots come for plumbing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of plumbing before robots. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe people want a person they trust in the house for a while longer. Maybe the business does the installing of the robots instead. I'd rather face the robots with a trade than with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your colleagues about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, yes, because she's been good to me. The others, no. I wouldn't want anyone thinking I'd given up before I had to.

say: People should look after their own, **families and communities** first.
I'd tell young lads to **learn a trade**, fast, rather than shout for **handouts**.
think: I'd be **out of software** within two years, since my job is all thinking work.
My dad's **plumbing business** is a hands-on door open until about 2031.

fieldNote: Karl's **family business** turns a fast AGI shock into a manageable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for families and firms to get ready, if they start now. Learn a trade, save, don't wait for someone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means a few more years of software pay, which I'd need, and then 2031. I could finish a plumbing qualification part-time by 2029 and step into my dad's business properly before AGI even lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the payroll job and learn the AI tools once they're in use on the team. I'd do the plumbing course two evenings a week and Saturdays with Dad, starting next autumn. Paula and I would still get engaged, but we'd save for a house deposit with my dad's firm in mind, not a city job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. It feels like a long apprenticeship more than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take over your dad's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With my brother, maybe. My brother is the better plumber, and I'm the one who'd sort out the computers and the paperwork. Between us, that's a proper firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does working two jobs for years worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be tiring. Paula would see less of me. But my dad worked six days a week for thirty years, and nobody gave him an easier deal.

Learn a trade, **save**, and don't wait for someone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the market will sort out a lot of it. People will move into new work. Families and firms just need to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in software most of that time, maybe make the next pay band or two. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. My dad would be retiring by then, and I'd think hard about stepping into the business with my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the payroll company and pick up the AI tools as they become normal, over the next couple of years. I'd save steadily for a house with Paula. Around 2032 I'd start the plumbing qualification, if the software work's starting to slip by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. It's on my mind, but it doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Paula change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd get engaged next year, probably marry the year after, and try for kids before thirty-two. With ten years, normal life carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you leave the plumbing too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the risk. Dad won't be around to teach me plumbing forever. Maybe I'd do Saturdays with him from 2028 anyway, just to keep my hand in.

Families and firms just need to be **sensible**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a way out through my dad's firm, but on trainee money, with three years before robots come for that too. What would help is proper adult apprenticeships, paid by the companies cutting jobs, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it means for families. My dad spent his life making sure I'd have an office job. My dad might end up being the one who saves my career, with a spanner.

headlineQuote: My dad might end up being the one who saves my career, with a spanner.
portrait: Karl, 27, works on the **payslip team** of a company making payroll software for small businesses.
He's on **low pay** with two weeks of savings, splitting rent with Paula, a teaching assistant.
He picks up AI tools **once they're proven** and keeps them away from tax tables.
His fallback is his dad's **plumbing business**, which he starts training in as change speeds up.
He believes in markets and family support, and wants firms that cut jobs to fund **adult apprenticeships**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: a way out through his dad's firm, but on trainee money.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** paid for by the companies cutting jobs, not handouts.
